topic: Spring request validation: DTO constraints versus business invariants
tomorrowTopic: Centralizing REST validation errors with Problem Details

hook.headline: @Valid cannot enforce every rule
hook.hook: Bean Validation is strong for request-local constraints; rules that depend on domain state or other records belong deeper in the application.
hook.visualCaption: Shape at the edge. Invariants where the required context exists.

mentalModel.title: Different rules need different context
mentalModel.coreIdea: Spring MVC can trigger Bean Validation on a request DTO, but those constraints should usually describe the submitted value itself. Business invariants that require repository state, authorization context, or cross-aggregate decisions belong in application/domain logic.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Keep malformed or locally invalid input out early without forcing stateful business decisions into DTO validators.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: validate what the request is at the edge; validate what it means where the state lives

code.title: Keep stateful rules out of the DTO
code.intro: The DTO handles request-local constraints; the service checks the uniqueness invariant with repository context.
code.highlightReason: Uniqueness depends on persisted state, so the service evaluates it using repository context rather than pretending it is a request-shape property.
code.takeaway: Use Bean Validation for declarative, request-local constraints; enforce state-dependent rules where the required domain context is available.
code.professionalNote: An exists-then-insert check alone is race-prone. If email uniqueness must hold under concurrency, back the invariant with a database UNIQUE constraint and translate violations appropriately.

production.title: Validation that survives concurrency
production.scenario: A registration endpoint rejects blank emails and must also prevent two users from claiming the same normalized email.
problems: Putting repository calls inside DTO validators couples transport validation to persistence.
Checking existsByEmail before insert does not make uniqueness atomic under concurrent requests.
production.professionalApproach: Use DTO constraints for syntactic/local checks, normalize deliberately, enforce the business rule in the service, and use a PostgreSQL UNIQUE constraint as the concurrency-safe final guard.
production.debugClue: If duplicate rows appear despite a pre-check, inspect the database constraint and concurrent insert path; the application-level existence query is not an atomic uniqueness guarantee.

interview.question: Where should validation live in a Spring Boot REST application?
interview.answer: Use request DTO Bean Validation for constraints that can be decided from the submitted values, such as blank fields or format rules. Put stateful or domain-specific invariants in application/domain logic where repositories and business context are available. When an invariant must hold under concurrency, enforce it at the database level too when the database can express it.
remember: Database constraints protect expressible invariants under races
